what_its_for: Dibasic sodium phosphate is used to relieve constipation, clean out your bowel before a colonoscopy or surgery, and sometimes to treat low phosphate levels in your blood. It works by drawing water into your intestines to help soften stools and trigger a bowel movement.
how_to_take: Take this medicine exactly as your doctor or pharmacist tells you. If you are taking tablets, swallow them whole with a full glass of water (at least 8 ounces). If you are using an enema, lie on your left side with your knees bent, gently insert the tip into your rectum, and slowly squeeze the bottle until it is empty. Stay in position for a few minutes before going to the bathroom. Drink plenty of water or clear fluids during treatment to stay hydrated.
dosing: The dose depends on why you are using this medicine and what form you are taking. For constipation relief with an enema, adults typically use one standard enema (4.5 oz) as a single dose. For bowel prep tablets (OsmoPrep), a common regimen is 32 tablets taken in split doses the evening before and morning of your procedure, each with 8 oz of water. For low phosphate levels, your doctor will set a specific dose. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and are using this medicine for low phosphate levels, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are using it for a bowel prep before a procedure, contact your doctor or clinic right away for instructions, as timing is very important.
storage: Store tablets and liquid forms at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not freeze the liquid or enema form. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking other laxatives or enemas at the same time unless your doctor tells you to. Do not use this medicine more often or in larger amounts than prescribed, as too much phosphate can be dangerous. Avoid eating a large meal right before a bowel prep. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, because some drugs like antacids, vitamins with calcium or magnesium, and certain blood pressure medicines can interact with this product. Avoid in people with kidney problems unless specifically directed by a doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: no bowel movement within 6 hours after using an enema or laxative, severe stomach pain or cramping, bloody stools, signs of dehydration such as dizziness, little or no urination, or extreme thirst, muscle weakness, irregular heartbeat, confusion, or seizures. These can be signs of a serious electrolyte imbalance. Also call your doctor if you need to use a laxative more than once a week, as this may signal a bigger health problem.
when_it_works: For constipation, an enema usually works within 2 to 15 minutes. Oral tablets used for constipation or bowel prep typically produce a bowel movement within 30 minutes to 6 hours. For low phosphate levels, it may take several days to weeks of regular use before your blood levels return to normal. Your doctor may check your blood levels during treatment.
special_populations: Children: Use only under a doctor's supervision. Do not use adult-strength enemas in children under 12. Older adults (65+): Use with extra caution, as elderly patients are more sensitive to fluid and electrolyte changes. Kidney disease: This medicine can be very dangerous if you have kidney problems. Talk to your doctor before using it. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Ask your doctor before using, especially for bowel prep, to make sure it is safe for you and your baby. Heart disease: Use with caution as electrolyte shifts can affect heart rhythm.
